Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**`git merge`** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has two parents. Existing commits are untouched.

```
Before:              After `git merge main` (on feature):
A---B---C  main      A---B---C-------  main
     \                    \           \
      D---E  feature       D---E---M  feature
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits one by one on top of the target branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History ends up linear, as if you'd started your work from the latest tip.

```
Before:              After `git rebase main` (on feature):
A---B---C  main      A---B---C  main
     \                        \
      D---E  feature           D'---E'  feature
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves what actually happened, including branch structure | Rewritten into a straight line |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for every replayed commit |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Possibly resolved repeatedly, once per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No, since it rewrites commits others may have based work on |
| Undoing | Revert or reset the merge commit | Recover the old tip via `git reflog` |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase local, unpushed work to tidy it up or bring it up to date with `main`.
- Merge when bringing a finished branch into a shared branch, or whenever the branch is already public.
- Don't rebase commits that other people have pulled. Their history will diverge from yours, and you'll need a force push (`git push --force-with-lease`) to publish the result.

A common workflow combines both: rebase your feature branch onto `main` to keep it current, then merge it into `main` when it's done.
